common_name: Dorana Sea Buckthorn (Compact German Early-Ripening Seaberry)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun on lean, sandy soil; Dorana is a female cultivar and needs a male sea buckthorn such as 'Pollmix' within pollinating distance.

directions: Dorana was introduced around 1990 by German breeder H.-J. Albrecht as a smaller, slower-growing sea buckthorn suited to home gardens rather than orchard rows, forming an upright shrub with relatively few suckers and spines compared to older commercial selections. Its medium-large orange berries ripen early and are reported to hold their color and firmness on the branch through much of the winter, while also testing among the highest in vitamin C of any named cultivar. Plant it in full sun on lean, well-drained, even sandy soil, since like all sea buckthorn it fixes its own nitrogen and resents rich or waterlogged ground. As a female clone it needs a male sea buckthorn growing nearby for wind pollination and fruit set.
sources: Agroforestry Research Trust — Sea Buckthorn Cultivars

common_name: Sadova No. 1 Schisandra (Self-Fertile Ukrainian Five-Flavor Berry)

planting.note: Plant softwood cuttings or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil and provide a sturdy trellis; unlike the wild species, a single Sadova No. 1 vine can set fruit without a separate male plant.

directions: Selected by Ivan Shaitan at the M.M. Gryshko National Botanic Garden in Kyiv, Ukraine, and entered into the state register in 1998, Sadova No. 1 was the first schisandra cultivar bred specifically for self-fertility, meaning a single vine can produce the small, tart-sweet red berries without a separate male pollinator as the wild dioecious species requires. It is also reported to be more productive and more tolerant of harsh weather swings than ungrafted wild-collected plants, making it a more reliable choice for home growers who only have room for one vine. Train the twining stems on a trellis, arbor, or fence in cool, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil with afternoon shade in hot climates, since the vine is a woodland understory plant by nature. Berries ripen in hanging clusters in late summer and are used fresh, dried, or in tinctures for their distinctive sweet-sour-salty-bitter-pungent flavor.
sources: M.M. Gryshko National Botanic Garden, Kyiv — cultivar registration records
Phytochemical and biotechnological studies on Schisandra chinensis cv. Sadova No. 1 (PMC5959991)

common_name: Silver Totem Buffaloberry (Columnar Plant Select Silver Buffaloberry)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; all Silver Totem plants are female clones and need a male silver buffaloberry within about 50 ft for wind pollination and fruit set.

directions: Discovered as a naturally narrow, upright seedling in a field of ordinary silver buffaloberry at Little Valley Wholesale Nursery in Brighton, Colorado in 2008, Silver Totem keeps the species' silvery foliage and tart red fruit but grows as a tight column 8 to 12 feet tall and only about 3 feet wide, useful as a narrow accent, screen, or colonnade where the spreading, thorny wild form would be too wide. It was introduced through the Plant Select program and shares the species' extreme drought and cold tolerance, thriving in lean, alkaline soils across the Great Plains and Intermountain West. Because every Silver Totem plant is a female clone, a male silver buffaloberry must be planted nearby for pollination and berry production. It is deer-resistant and needs little care beyond occasional shaping.

common_name: Alfredo American Highbush Cranberry (Compact Bailey Nurseries Cranberrybush)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; fruit set is heaviest with a second Viburnum trilobum cultivar planted nearby.

directions: Selected at Bailey Nurseries as a naturally dense, compact sport of American highbush cranberry, Alfredo matures at only 5 to 6 feet tall and wide, roughly half the size of the species, which makes it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller home landscapes. It carries the same lacy white spring flower clusters, bright red translucent fall and winter fruit, and brilliant red autumn foliage as the full-sized shrub, and the fruit can be used the same way in jellies and sauces once past the first hard frost. Growers also report somewhat better resistance to the aphids that commonly disfigure the species' new growth. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade, and site a second cranberrybush viburnum nearby for the most reliable fruit set.

common_name: Redwing American Highbush Cranberry (J.N. Select Heavy-Fruiting Cranberrybush)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; it sets some fruit on its own but yields are heaviest with a second cranberrybush viburnum blooming nearby.

directions: Selected by Michael Yanny of Johnson's Nursery in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin, and introduced in 1983, J.N. Select was chosen for its densely branched, upright-rounded form, vigorous growth, and new foliage that emerges red-tinted before maturing green and then turning brilliant red again in fall. In mid- to late spring it carries the species' flat white flower clusters, followed by heavy, long-lasting clusters of bright red fruit that persist from late fall into winter and can be harvested after frost for jelly or left for winter birds. It is more floriferous and fruitful than many seed-grown highbush cranberries and, while somewhat self-fruitful, sets its heaviest crops with another cranberrybush viburnum planted nearby. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates clay and periodic wet feet better than most fruiting shrubs.
sources: Chicagoland Grows — Redwing American Cranberrybush Viburnum

common_name: Yezberry Honey Bunch Honeyberry (Compact Japanese Haskap)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring within about 50 feet of another Yezberry selection, since Honey Bunch needs a different haskap cultivar nearby for best fruit set.

directions: Honey Bunch (cultivar code 'Kaido', US Plant Patent PP28,662) is a compact, purely Japanese-type haskap sold under the Proven Winners Yezberry label, reaching only about 3 to 5 feet tall and wide, which makes it one of the more manageable honeyberries for small yards or mixed shrub borders. Like other Yezberry selections it flowers very early in spring with small yellow blooms that become elongated, sweet blue fruit well suited to fresh eating, baking, or processing. It needs a different Yezberry or compatible haskap cultivar planted nearby to cross-pollinate, since isolated plants set little fruit. Grow it in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil; established plants tolerate winter cold well below 0F but, like most haskap, struggle in hot, humid summer climates.
sources: Proven Winners — Yezberry Honey Bunch Japanese Haskap
US Plant Patent PP28,662 — Lonicera caerulea 'Kaido'

common_name: Boreal Bliss Honeyberry (University of Saskatchewan Wild-Canadian-Parentage Haskap)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring in full sun; plant a compatible haskap cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Released from the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program under Bob Bors, Boreal Bliss is notable as the first named haskap cultivar to carry wild Canadian Lonicera caerulea in its parentage alongside the Japanese and Russian lines behind most earlier Boreal-series releases. Breeders selected it over several years of trials for consistently heavy, good-flavored fruit; the elongated berries taper to a distinct point at the flower end, a trait breeders use to distinguish it from the similar, more rounded 'Boreal Beast'. Like other University of Saskatchewan haskaps it blooms very early in spring and needs a compatible cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and full fruit set. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; the extreme winter hardiness typical of the breeding program should extend well into USDA zone 2.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program — 'Boreal Bliss' cultivar notes
Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Haskap Breeding Program
